name: Financials and supply chain
answer: These measures show the money and equipment behind the buildout: what the largest builders spend, what colocation space rents for, and how long critical equipment takes to arrive. Capital spending by a handful of companies sets the pace of AI data center construction.

metrics.line: Quarterly capital spending reported to the SEC by the companies building the facilities, tracked on this page from each company's own XBRL filings.
metrics.label: Hyperscaler and colocation capital expenditure

metrics.line: Market rate per kilowatt per month for leased capacity, the price signal for scarcity in each metro.
metrics.label: Colocation rental rates

metrics.line: Order-to-delivery time for transformers, switchgear, generators, cooling plant, and high-end accelerators.
metrics.label: Critical equipment lead times

reading.body:
Capital spending by a handful of companies sets the pace of AI data center construction. The eight operators listed here report quarterly figures that range from under a billion dollars to more than fifty billion, and that spread is the story.

Amazon leads at 54.2 billion dollars for the quarter ending June 2026, followed by Alphabet at 35.7 billion, Microsoft at 30.9 billion, and Oracle at 28.5 billion. Meta reports 19.0 billion and CoreWeave 7.7 billion. The two colocation landlords, Equinix at 1.26 billion and Digital Realty at 870 million, sit an order of magnitude below the hyperscalers. The gap reflects different businesses: the large figures cover owned and leased capacity across whole portfolios, while the smaller ones are the reported capital spending of firms that lease space rather than build for themselves.

For AI specifically, this is the money that becomes buildings and power connections. A quarter of spending at this scale has to land somewhere as land, shell, transformers, and grid interconnection, which is why the equipment lead times tracked alongside these figures matter as much as the dollar totals. The figures do not show how much of each company's spending goes to AI rather than cloud, search, or retail infrastructure, and they do not show where the facilities are sited or whether the power to run them has been secured. They also cover only these eight operators, so the total buildout is larger than what is listed here.
